clue.text: Title boxing gentleman coveted

indicators.note: boxing means holding inside, as a box holds its contents, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a deed is a title, as in a title deed proving ownership
Sir is the form of address for a gentleman

explanation.surface: A man of rank wanted something badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Title' looks like a rank to go with the gentleman, but here it is the legal document, a title deed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something coveted is wished for intensely, the same as being longed for.

clue.text: It raises awareness, in a sense

definitions.text: It raises awareness, in a sense

parts.words: It raises awareness, in a sense
parts.note: read literally, a device that increases what a person can perceive through one of the senses, namely hearing

explanation.definitionFit: A hearing device amplifies sound, literally making the wearer more aware through the sense of hearing.

clue.text: States views and positions

indicators.note: states means says, so the word for views is to be spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: views are sights, things seen

explanation.surface: A list of countries' opinions and stances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'States' looks like nations or a verb meaning declares, and it is the latter: it signals saying 'sights' aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: Sites are locations or places where something is set.

clue.text: Show's on about now

parts.note: re means on or about, in the sense of concerning
the present is now, the current moment

explanation.surface: A programme is concerned with current affairs.
explanation.definitionFit: To represent is to depict or portray, so a show that represents something depicts it.

clue.text: Belief in de Sade is madness

indicators.note: in tells us the letters lie inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Claims that the Marquis de Sade's thinking was insane.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the end of 'Sade', all of 'is' and the start of 'madness'.
explanation.definitionFit: Deism is a belief in a creator god who does not intervene in the world.

clue.text: Senseless when I have one over the eight

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as he arrived'
one more than eight is nine; the phrase is also British slang for slightly drunk

explanation.surface: Acting foolishly after having one drink too many.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One over the eight' is British slang for being tipsy, which suits the surface, but here it is plain arithmetic.
explanation.definitionFit: Asinine means stupid, as foolish as a donkey, so without sense.

clue.text: Can — missing round — be sober

indicators.note: round means going about the outside, so the word for missing surrounds the word for can

parts.note: absent means missing
a tin is a can

explanation.surface: Turning down a round at the pub keeps you sober.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like a verb, and 'missing round' like skipping a round of drinks; instead the tin is put round by ABSENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who abstains from drink is teetotal and therefore stays sober.

clue.text: Cool house with a grand bathroom

parts.note: a means one, which the Roman numeral I gives
G is short for grand, a thousand pounds
loo is British slang for a lavatory or bathroom

explanation.surface: A trendy home that has an impressive bathroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cool' looks like trendy, but the house really is cold: it is built of snow.
explanation.definitionFit: An Inuit snow dwelling is literally a cold home.

clue.text: Folly — losing recipe for sauce

indicators.note: losing means a letter is dropped from the word for folly

parts.note: imprudence is folly, a lack of good sense
R is the abbreviation for recipe, from Latin recipe on prescriptions

explanation.surface: A culinary blunder: leaving out the instructions for a sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sauce' looks culinary, alongside 'recipe', but it means cheek.
explanation.definitionFit: Sauce is British slang for cheek or insolence, which is rudeness.

clue.text: Back last nag — not the first

parts.note: the end is the last part

indicators.note: not the first means the opening letter of the word for nag is dropped

parts.note: a nag is a horse, especially a poor one

explanation.surface: Advice to a punter: support the horse in last place, not the leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like betting on a horse, which suits 'nag', but it is the definition, meaning support.
explanation.definitionFit: To endorse a proposal is to support or back it.

clue.text: End-of-term examinations

parts.note: looks like school tests at the close of a term; read instead as inspections made when a life's term has ended

explanation.definitionFit: Post-mortem inspections are made on a body after death, the end of one's term of life.

clue.text: Fat detective in a hat

indicators.note: in places the word for detective inside the word for a hat

parts.note: lid is slang for a hat
PI is a private investigator, a detective

explanation.surface: An overweight sleuth in a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fat' looks like an adjective describing the detective, but it is the definition, a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Lipids are the class of biological molecules that includes fats and oils.

clue.text: "I will", shortly to be heard here

indicators.note: to be heard means the shortened phrase is spoken, giving a word of the same sound

parts.note: I will shortened is the contraction I'll

explanation.surface: Where the wedding vow 'I will' is soon to be spoken.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition 'here' points to the church passage where a couple stand to make their vows, saying 'I will'.
explanation.definitionFit: The wedding vow is said at the altar end of the church walkway, so 'here' is that place.

clue.text: Mum's almost sick getting degree by post

parts.note: ma is a word for mum

indicators.note: almost means the word for sick loses its last letter

parts.note: ill means sick
an order is a rank or degree, as in a high order

explanation.surface: Mother is nearly ill after earning a qualification through the post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Degree' looks like a university qualification, suiting correspondence courses, but here it means rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods bought through mail order are sent by post.

clue.text: Priest due to convert? Shame!

indicators.note: convert means change into another form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A clergyman is set to change faith, a scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Convert' suggests religion, apt beside 'Priest', but signals rearranging the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring someone into disrepute is to bring shame or dishonour on them.

clue.text: Ambling through with smart outside drive

indicators.note: outside means the word for smart wraps round the word for drive

parts.note: to smart is to sting, feel a sharp pain
roll can mean drive or propel, as in rolling a car along

explanation.surface: Walking slowly while going through a stylish driveway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart' looks like stylish and 'drive' like a driveway; they are a sting and to roll.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambling and strolling both describe walking at a leisurely pace.

clue.text: Bare? It's apt in nude frolic

indicators.note: a frolic is lively play, so the letters romp into a new order

explanation.surface: Is naked play fitting for a nude romp?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks 'Bare' as a stretch: an unpainted surface is bare of paint.
explanation.definitionFit: An unpainted wall or board is bare, left without a coat of colour.

clue.text: Oz is a cool cat

definitions.meaning: oz is the abbreviation for a unit of weight equal to a sixteenth of a pound
the snow leopard, a big cat of cold mountains, is another name for this animal

explanation.surface: Australia is a laid-back place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oz' looks like Australia and 'cool cat' like a hip person; one is the weight abbreviation and the other a snow leopard, cool because it lives in the snow.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit of weight (abbreviated oz) and a snow leopard share this name.

clue.text: Fine memorial flying French flag

indicators.note: flying suggests letters scattered by the wind, so they are rearranged

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A good memorial has a French flag flying over it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flying' looks like what a flag does, but it signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: The oriflamme was the red-gold banner of the medieval kings of France, a royal standard.

clue.text: A cad following first-class degree of purity

indicators.note: following means the article and the cad come after the letter from class
first takes just the opening letter of the word class

parts.note: a rat is a cad, a contemptible man

explanation.surface: A scoundrel comes behind the top student in a test of purity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First-class' looks like a top grade; here it is read as the first of 'class'.
explanation.definitionFit: The carat measures the fineness of gold, how pure it is in twenty-fourths.

clue.text: Party in charge is a bore

indicators.note: in places the political party inside the word for charge

parts.note: care is charge, as in being in someone's care
Lib is short for Liberal, a political party

explanation.surface: The governing party is dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bore' looks like a tedious thing, but it is the diameter of a gun barrel.
explanation.definitionFit: The bore of a gun is its internal diameter, measured as its calibre.

clue.text: Square with Epstein's sculpture "insignificance"

indicators.note: a sculpture reshapes its material, so these letters are remodelled

parts.note: a T-square is a drawing square, so T can stand for it
the name and its S are taken as written; Jacob Epstein was a sculptor

explanation.surface: A town square holds an Epstein statue titled with an abstract word.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacob Epstein was a noted British sculptor, so 'sculpture' sits naturally while signalling an anagram of T and EPSTEINS.
explanation.definitionFit: Pettiness is smallness, the quality of being trivial or unimportant.

clue.text: Rubber — south leading clubs with our queen

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games
taken as written
ER, Elizabeth Regina, stands for the Queen

explanation.surface: A bridge rubber: South leads clubs, with our queen in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubber' looks like a set of bridge games, fitting 'south' and 'clubs', but it is something that rubs.
explanation.definitionFit: A scourer is a pad used to scrub pans, so it rubs them clean.

clue.text: Strains to send the kids off

definitions.text: Strains to send the kids off

parts.words: Strains to send the kids off
parts.note: strains look like efforts, but they are tunes; sending off is putting to sleep

explanation.definitionFit: Soft bedtime songs are sung to children to make them fall asleep.

clue.text: Point of view may be obtuse

definitions.meaning: a perspective or slant on a matter
a corner between two lines can measure more than ninety degrees

explanation.surface: An opinion that might be dim-witted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obtuse' looks like slow-witted, but in geometry it describes a measure between 90 and 180 degrees.
explanation.definitionFit: A perspective and a geometric corner between two lines both share this name.

clue.text: Very fine shave for the auditor

indicators.note: an auditor is a listener, so the word is the one heard, not seen

parts.note: to shear is to cut or shave, as wool from sheep

explanation.surface: A barber offers a close shave to a listener.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' looks like an accountant, but it means a hearer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheer fabric is delicately thin and transparent.

clue.text: Dance where you'll end up under the bar!

definitions.text: Dance where you'll end up under the bar!

parts.words: Dance where you'll end up under the bar!
parts.note: a pub joke on being drunk under the bar, describing a party dance where you pass beneath a pole

explanation.definitionFit: In this Caribbean dance, people bend backwards to pass beneath a lowering pole.

clue.text: Bug, say, not lit up

indicators.note: up in a down entry means the run of both pieces is read from bottom to top

parts.note: eg, for example, is said here as 'say'
dim means not lit, poorly illuminated

explanation.surface: A bug, perhaps, that isn't glowing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' in a down entry turns the whole run EGDIM, from 'say' and 'not lit', to read bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny biting fly is an insect, loosely called a bug.

clue.text: First boy band. Take…?

indicators.note: first takes only the opening letter of the word boy

parts.note: a ring is a band, as worn on a finger

explanation.surface: Debut boy band: take one?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take' is offered with a question mark because bring and take are opposite directions of carrying.
explanation.definitionFit: Bring and take are related verbs of carrying, toward and away from the speaker.

clue.text: Old French season seafood dish?

definitions.meaning: the eleventh month of the French Revolutionary calendar, in high summer
lobster cooked in a creamy sauce bears this name

explanation.surface: An old French dish of seafood for the time of year.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark notes the dish is lobster thermidor, the word being only part of its name.
explanation.definitionFit: A summer month of the Revolutionary calendar and a creamy lobster preparation share this name.

clue.text: E's a genius!

parts.note: the letter E is the first letter, the head, of the word egg

explanation.surface: A claim that a person called E is brilliant.
explanation.walkthrough: Reverse clue: E is the head of EGG, so 'E's a' describes the answer read as two words.
explanation.definitionFit: An intellectual is mocked as a brainy type, a genius.

clue.text: Animal mounted here, say, in the east end

indicators.note: spoken in a Cockney accent, as in London's East End, with the H dropped

parts.note: mounted means rode, and here dropped of its H becomes 'ere

explanation.surface: An animal ridden here, spoken in a London accent.
explanation.walkthrough: The East End of London is home to the Cockney accent, which drops initial H, so 'rode 'ere' sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A small European deer is a wild animal.
